lessons.title: What HIV and AIDS are and how HIV spreads
lessons.html:
What HIV and AIDS are

HIV is the Human Immunodeficiency Virus. It attacks the body's defence system (the immune system), which normally fights sickness. AIDS is the late stage of HIV when the immune system is very weak and the person gets serious infections such as TB and pneumonia.

A person can have HIV for years and look and feel healthy. The only way to know your status is to test. Testing is free and confidential at government clinics, and many farms and abattoirs arrange testing days.

How HIV spreads

  • Sex without a condom with a person who has HIV.
  • Blood to blood contact, for example sharing needles or razors, or a cut touching infected blood.
  • From a mother to her baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding, if she is not on treatment.

How HIV does NOT spread

  • Shaking hands, hugging or working side by side.
  • Sharing cups, plates, toilets or showers.
  • Mosquito or tick bites.
  • Eating meat or food prepared by a person with HIV.

Protecting yourself

  • Use a condom every time you have sex. Condoms are free at clinics.
  • Reduce the number of sexual partners.
  • Do not share razors or needles.
  • Get tested, and ask your partner to test too.
  • Get checked and treated for other sexually transmitted infections. They make it easier to get HIV.

Treatment works

There is no cure yet, but antiretroviral treatment (ARVs) keeps the virus under control. A person who takes ARVs every day as the clinic tells them can live a long, healthy and working life. When the virus is kept very low, it is not passed on through sex. Pregnant women on treatment can protect their babies.

lessons.title: HIV at work: safety, rights and support
lessons.html:
HIV at work

Safety with blood at work

In an abattoir or on a farm, cuts happen. The risk of getting HIV at work is low, but always treat all human blood as if it may carry infection.

  • When helping an injured co-worker, wear gloves from the first aid box before touching blood.
  • Cover your own cuts with a waterproof plaster.
  • Clean blood spills with gloves and the cleaning solution your workplace uses.
  • If someone else's blood gets into your cut, eyes or mouth, wash it at once with plenty of water and report it to your supervisor immediately. Go to the clinic the same day. Medicine called PEP can lower the chance of infection, but it must be started as soon as possible and within 72 hours.

Rights at work

  • Your HIV status is private. You do not have to tell your employer. If you tell someone, they must keep it confidential.
  • It is against the law to treat a worker unfairly because of HIV status. The Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998 protects workers against unfair discrimination, including on HIV status.
  • An employer may not make you take an HIV test as a condition of getting or keeping a job, unless it has been allowed by the Labour Court.
  • A worker with HIV who can do the job keeps the job, like any other worker.

Supporting each other

  • Do not gossip or make jokes about HIV.
  • Treat co-workers living with HIV with respect.
  • Encourage friends to test and to keep taking their treatment.
  • Know where your nearest clinic is and what help your workplace offers, such as a wellness programme or peer educators.

Key points

  • HIV spreads through unprotected sex, blood and from mother to baby, not by everyday contact.
  • Test to know your status. Testing is free and confidential at clinics.
  • ARVs taken every day keep people healthy and working.
  • Use gloves for blood and report any blood exposure at once.
  • HIV status is private and unfair discrimination is against the law.
